title: Glacial Deposition & a Glaciated Upland: The Lake District
description: Erratics, drumlins and moraines — and how the Lake District's landscape tells the full glacial story.
content_html:
Why Glaciers Deposit Material

Throughout its journey, a glacier carries enormous quantities of rock debris — fragments shattered by freeze-thaw, blocks ripped out by plucking, material scraped from valley floors and walls by abrasion, and rock falls from valley sides onto the glacier's surface. All this material is transported within the ice and at its base. When the glacier begins to melt — either at its snout where it reaches warmer temperatures, or at the end of an ice age when the climate warms — it loses the energy to carry this load and deposits it. The speed of deposition and the way water is involved determines whether the resulting sediment is till (unsorted, dumped directly from the ice) or outwash (sorted and layered, deposited by meltwater streams beyond the ice front). Till is the most diagnostic deposit — its total lack of sorting, with clay and boulders mixed indiscriminately, tells geologists immediately that ice, not water, put it there.

Erratics

An erratic is a boulder or block of rock that is completely different from the bedrock on which it rests — because the glacier carried it from a distant source and dropped it when the ice melted. Erratics are dramatic evidence of ice movement. The Norber erratics in the Yorkshire Dales are Silurian greywacke boulders sitting on much younger Carboniferous limestone pavements — the ice carried them uphill from the south and deposited them on the limestone pavement. The limestone pavement has been dissolved away around the protected bases of the boulders, leaving them perched on limestone pedestals up to 50 cm high. By matching erratic rock types to their source quarries, geologists can map the exact direction and distance of ice flow during the last ice age.

Key Fact

The Norber erratics in the Yorkshire Dales are Silurian greywacke boulders sitting on Carboniferous limestone — deposited by a glacier that carried them uphill from a different rock source. Matching erratic rock types to their source lets geologists map ice-flow direction.

Drumlins

Drumlins are smooth, oval-shaped hills of glacial till with a distinctive asymmetric profile: the stoss (upstream) end is blunt, steep and high; the lee (downstream) end tapers gently in the direction of ice flow. They range from a few metres high and 100 m long to 50 m high and over 1 km long. Their exact formation is still debated, but the accepted mechanism is that the moving glacier moulded pre-existing till into streamlined shapes aligned with the ice flow, possibly around a harder core of rock or lodged boulder. Drumlins are rarely found alone — they occur in swarms called basket-of-eggs topography. The Eden Valley in Cumbria has one of England's best examples of a drumlin swarm: dozens of smooth elongated hills rising from the valley floor, all oriented in the same direction showing the southward flow of ice from the Lake District fells.

Types of Moraine

Moraine is the collective term for till deposited in specific positions by a glacier. There are four main types. Lateral moraine forms along the sides of a valley glacier as freeze-thaw debris from the valley walls falls onto the glacier's edges and is carried along. When the glacier retreats, lateral moraine is left as a ridge running parallel to the old glacier margins, high on the valley sides. Medial moraine forms when two valley glaciers merge: their lateral moraines meet and form a dark streak of debris running down the centre of the combined glacier. When the ice melts, medial moraine is left as a low ridge in the middle of the valley. Terminal moraine (or end moraine) marks the furthest point reached by a glacier — material bulldozed ahead and deposited at the snout forms a curved ridge across the valley floor. It marks the limit of glacial advance like a physical bookmark in the landscape. Recessional moraines are smaller ridges deposited at successive positions as the glacier retreats in stages, each marking a pause in the retreat. A glacier's ground moraine is the sheet of till deposited across the whole valley floor as the glacier melts.

Position is the key. Lateral moraine runs parallel to the valley walls, high on the slope. Medial moraine runs down the middle of the valley floor as a low ridge. Terminal moraine forms a curved arc across the valley, blocking drainage (sometimes creating a moraine-dammed lake behind it). Recessional moraines are a series of parallel ridges getting further from the source. All moraine is made of till — unsorted boulders, pebbles and clay — which distinguishes it from river or wind deposits that are sorted by grain size.

Key Fact

The four moraine types: lateral (sides of glacier), medial (middle, where two glaciers merge), terminal (furthest advance), recessional (pauses in retreat). All are made of unsorted till deposited directly from ice, not meltwater.

Case Study: The Lake District

The Lake District in Cumbria, England's largest national park (2,362 km²), provides a complete glacial landscape — both erosional and depositional landforms are visible at every scale. The central dome of ancient Borrowdale Volcanic rocks provided the source area for multiple corrie glaciers that later merged into a major valley glacier system radiating outwards in all directions.

Erosional landforms: Corries are found on the north and northeast faces of the main fells — Red Tarn corrie sits at 720 m below Helvellyn's eastern face, its backwall rising over 300 m. Striding Edge and Swirral Edge are the arêtes bordering Red Tarn on either side. The major valleys — Borrowdale, Langdale, Wasdale and Ennerdale — are classic glacial troughs with flat floors, near-vertical sides and truncated spurs. The ribbon lakes that fill their floors are some of England's largest: Windermere (18 km, 64 m deep), Ullswater (12 km), Coniston Water and Wastwater (the deepest at 79 m). Aira Force waterfall near Ullswater drops from a hanging valley left by a smaller tributary glacier.

Depositional landforms: The Eden Valley to the east of the Lake District contains an extensive drumlin swarm — tens of smooth oval till mounds aligned to show southward ice flow. Terminal and recessional moraines cross the lowland valleys at the edge of the national park, marking successive positions of the retreating glacier snouts after the last ice age maximum. Ground moraine covers the valley floors throughout the park — the rich farmland of the Vale of Keswick sits on glacial till. The Bowder Stone in Borrowdale, a large boulder of andesite lava from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, is traditionally cited as an erratic but is now considered by geologists to be a rockfall from Bowder Crag directly above, dislodged after the glacier retreated.

In few places on Earth can you see so many glacial landforms within a day's walking. Stand on Helvellyn and you can see the corrie (Red Tarn) below, the arêtes (Striding Edge, Swirral Edge) on either side, and the glacial trough of Ullswater stretching north. Drive south and within 20 minutes you are in Langdale — another glacial trough, truncated spurs on either side, the flat trough floor now farmed, and the Langdale Pikes showing freeze-thaw-shattered summit ridges. The Lake District became England's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017, recognised partly for its glacially carved landscape.
exam_tip_html: For a question asking you to 'identify and explain glacial landforms in a named upland area' (6 marks), use the Lake District and split your answer into erosional (corries, arêtes, glacial troughs, ribbon lakes — with names: Red Tarn, Striding Edge, Windermere) and depositional (drumlins in the Eden Valley, moraines, Norber erratics in the Yorkshire Dales). Examiners reward specific place names and the link between process and landform. Avoid listing without explaining why each landform is there.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Glaciers deposit till (unsorted, directly from ice) and outwash (sorted by meltwater). Erratics (Norber, Yorkshire Dales) are rocks carried hundreds of kilometres from their source; drumlins (Eden Valley) are streamlined till mounds aligned with ice flow.
  • Four moraine types mark stages of glacial activity: lateral (valley sides), medial (where glaciers merge), terminal (furthest advance) and recessional (pauses in retreat).
  • The Lake District shows a complete glacial landscape: erosional landforms (Red Tarn corrie, Striding Edge arête, Windermere ribbon lake in a glacial trough, Aira Force hanging valley waterfall) alongside depositional landforms (Eden Valley drumlin swarm, moraines across the lowlands, Bowder Stone — a large andesite boulder traditionally cited as an erratic but now interpreted as a rockfall from Bowder Crag above).

glossary_terms.definition: Unsorted rock debris of all sizes, from clay particles to boulders, deposited directly by glacier ice rather than by meltwater.
A rock or boulder transported by a glacier from a distant source and deposited in an area of different bedrock, sometimes hundreds of kilometres from its origin.
A smooth, elongated hill made of glacial till, with a blunt upstream end and a tapered downstream end, formed and moulded beneath a moving glacier.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a ridge of till deposited at the furthest point reached by a glacier?
A) Lateral moraine
B) Medial moraine
C) Terminal moraine
D) Recessional moraine
Outline what makes an erratic distinctive from other glacial deposits.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per point with development. An erratic is a boulder of rock that is completely different from the bedrock it rests on — indicating it was transported by ice from a distant source. Named example: Norber erratics (Yorkshire Dales) — Silurian greywacke boulders on Carboniferous limestone, perched on pedestals up to 50 cm high where the surrounding limestone has been dissolved away.

practice_questions.text: Describe the characteristics of a drumlin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: asymmetric oval shape; blunt stoss (upstream) end is steep and high; tapered lee (downstream) end points in direction of ice flow; made entirely of unsorted till; found in swarms (basket-of-eggs topography); range from a few metres to 50 m high. Named example (Eden Valley, Cumbria). Secure: shape described with upstream/downstream distinction. Developing: oval and smooth but no asymmetry. Emerging: vague hill description.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between lateral, medial and terminal moraines.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: each type defined, positioned correctly and formation explained — lateral (debris falls from valley walls onto glacier edges, deposited as ridges parallel to old glacier margins); medial (where two glaciers merge, their lateral moraines join to form a central streak, left as a low ridge down the valley floor); terminal (material bulldozed to the snout marks the furthest glacial advance as a curved ridge across the valley). Each type's position and formation clearly linked. Named example for at least one. Secure: two types with explanation. Developing: all three named but poorly defined. Emerging: only one type.

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK upland, identify its major erosional and depositional glacial landforms.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Lake District named throughout; erosional landforms with names — Red Tarn corrie (rotational slip, armchair hollow), Striding Edge arête (two corries eroding back), Windermere ribbon lake (18 km, 64 m deep in glacial trough), Aira Force hanging valley waterfall; depositional — Eden Valley drumlin swarm (streamlined till mounds aligned with ice flow), Norber erratics in the Yorkshire Dales (Silurian greywacke on Carboniferous limestone, perched on pedestal up to 50 cm), terminal and recessional moraines across valley floors. Secure: two erosional and two depositional with names. Developing: names landforms without explanation. Emerging: named area, vague landforms.

practice_questions.text: 'Depositional landforms are as significant as erosional landforms in explaining the landscape of a glaciated upland.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument using the Lake District with a justified judgement. For depositional: Eden Valley drumlin swarm covers a vast area; till plains (ground moraine) form the valley-floor farming land; moraines dam ribbon lakes; Norber erratics (Yorkshire Dales) are a striking example of glacial transport. Against: the iconic Lake District views are all erosional — Helvellyn corries, arêtes, glacial troughs, ribbon lakes; the dramatic mountain topography is entirely erosional; deposition is less immediately visible. Reaches a judgement — erosional landforms are more visually dominant in the upland core, but depositional landforms cover a greater total area in the lowland fringe and valley floors and are essential for farming. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists landforms without judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What makes till different from outwash as a glacial deposit?
options: Till is unsorted; outwash is sorted by meltwater into layers
Till is deposited by meltwater; outwash is deposited directly by ice
Till only contains boulders; outwash only contains clay
They are the same material deposited in different seasons

knowledge_checks.q: Where are the Norber erratics, and why are they significant?
options: In the Eden Valley — they show the direction of glacier flow
In Borrowdale — they are the largest boulders in England
In the Yorkshire Dales — Silurian greywacke boulders on Carboniferous limestone, showing ice transported them uphill
In Snowdonia — granite boulders from Scotland deposited in Wales

knowledge_checks.q: The blunt, steep upstream end of a drumlin is called the _____ side.
The type of moraine that forms where two valley glaciers merge is called _____ moraine.
Match each moraine type to its correct position relative to the glacier.
right: Ridges of till deposited along the sides of a valley glacier, left high on valley walls after retreat
A curved ridge of till marking the furthest point ever reached by the glacier's snout
Smaller parallel ridges deposited at successive positions as the glacier paused during its retreat

flashcard_questions.a: Unsorted rock debris deposited directly by glacier ice — boulders and clay particles mixed together, not sorted by size.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between till and outwash?
flashcard_questions.a: Till is unsorted and deposited by ice; outwash is sorted into layers by meltwater streams beyond the glacier snout.
A boulder transported by a glacier from a distant source and left on bedrock of a completely different rock type.

Yorkshire Dales — Silurian greywacke boulders deposited on Carboniferous limestone by the glacier. The surrounding limestone has dissolved away, leaving the boulders perched on pedestals up to 50 cm high.
Smooth and oval, with a blunt steep stoss (upstream) end and a tapered lee (downstream) end pointing in the direction of ice flow.

flashcard_questions.q: Where is England's best example of a drumlin swarm?
flashcard_questions.a: The Eden Valley, Cumbria, where dozens of smooth till mounds are aligned showing southward ice flow.
Ridges of till deposited along the sides of a valley glacier, left high on valley walls when the ice retreats.
A curved ridge of till deposited at the furthest point reached by a glacier, marking the limit of its advance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between terminal and recessional moraine?
flashcard_questions.a: Terminal moraine marks the maximum advance; recessional moraines are smaller ridges left at pauses during retreat.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two erosional landforms and their location in the Lake District.
flashcard_questions.a: Red Tarn corrie (below Helvellyn) and Windermere ribbon lake (18 km long glacial trough).
A large boulder of andesite from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, long cited as a glacial erratic but now thought to be a rockfall from Bowder Crag above.

flashcard_questions.q: What do drumlins tell geologists about the glacier that deposited them?
flashcard_questions.a: Their tapered lee ends point in the direction of ice flow, mapping the path and direction of the glacier.
